refuter_findings.evidence: The current entry describes Teschl §9.1 and §9.6, pp. 181–186 and 214–221, as covering transfer matrices and transmission. The book’s contents place §9.6 at printed p. 209 and §9.7 at p. 214; these sections concern spectral transformations and spectra, not the cited transfer-matrix topic. The locator and description do not match the [current source](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf).

The current entry cites Binney and Skinner, Chapter 4, pp. 65–88, for rectangular-barrier transmission. In the [cited book](https://www-thphys.physics.ox.ac.uk/people/JamesBinney/qb.pdf), Chapter 4 begins at p. 58 and concerns transformations and observables; motion in step potentials is Chapter 5, with scattering in §5.3.

The current entry assigns finite-well negative eigenvalues, root conditions, and oscillation counting to Teschl §§9.1 and 9.6, including pp. 214–221. The book’s contents place §9.6 at p. 209 and §9.7 at p. 214; Theorem 9.40 in §9.7 concerns full-line eigenvalues below the essential spectrum, not this bounded-well root and count result. The [cited locator](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf) does not support the description.

The current entry cites Binney and Skinner, Chapter 4, pp. 65–88, for the finite square well. In the [cited book](https://www-thphys.physics.ox.ac.uk/people/JamesBinney/qb.pdf), the square-well treatment is Chapter 5, §5.1, pp. 75–79; Chapter 4 concerns transformations and observables.

The current entry describes Teschl §9.1, pp. 181–186, as supplying the interval Dirichlet nodal count. The [book](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf) identifies §9.1 as general Sturm–Liouville theory; its Theorem 9.40 nodal result is in §9.7 and has full-line hypotheses, not the bounded-interval Dirichlet hypotheses cited here.

The current entry cites Teschl Lemma 9.4, pp. 184–185, for Green kernels and resolvents. In the [cited text](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf), Lemma 9.4 computes the closure and adjoint domains of the minimal Sturm–Liouville operator; the Green-resolvent formula is Lemma 9.7 in §9.2.

The current entry cites Teschl §9.1, pp. 181–186, for separated boundary conditions and simplicity. The [book](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf) places Theorem 9.6 on separated boundary conditions in §9.2; §9.1 is the preceding Sturm–Liouville theory section.

The current entry cites Teschl §3.2, pp. 89–92, for Fourier and sine-basis completeness. The [book’s contents](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf) place §3.2 at printed p. 99 under measure theory, so the cited locator does not support that claim.

The current entry cites Teschl §9.2, pp. 187–193, for negative eigenvalues of point-interaction realizations. The [book](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-schroe/schroe.pdf) identifies §9.2 as Weyl limit-point/limit-circle theory and does not state the cited delta-interaction bound-state formula there.

The title says the zero-range model has “its unique bound state,” without qualifying the coupling. Statement (b) says that for every g ≥ 0 there is no negative eigenvalue and that 0 is not an eigenvalue; by the line-model definition, a bound state must have negative energy. For example, at g = 0 the stated model has no bound state. Uniqueness is established in statement (c) only for g < 0.

The example calls the barrier “classically forbidden at this energy,” but its stated model and dependencies supply the quantum line-model scattering calculation, not a definition of a classical allowed region or a classical particle energy relation for this barrier. U > E is explicit; the classical comparison is not defined. The model computation does not rely on this phrase, but the technical term needs a local definition or removal.
